TIGER AND BISON
HUNTING

label: text
text: STORIES OF MAN-EATERS: A CATTLE-LIFTER.

label: text
text: The following appeared as a letter in the daily "Statesman," Calcutta.—"Jungli Kooltra" writes.—Being very fond of shikar perhaps my own experiences will be of interest to other sportsmen. I am certainly not a "great shikari," but I am very keen; I love jungle life and do a big game shoot whenever I can arrange to go for one—not a very easy matter, however, nowa-diys.

label: text
text: Most of my shooting has been done in the Central Provinces, and as bison are preserved in most of the forests there, my experiences with bison are limited. But I have had some experiences with tigers, including a man-eater, which will perhaps be interesting.

label: text
text: In March last X and I went to the southern part of the Central Provinces, and it was suggested to us by the local authorities that we should go after a notorious man-enter which had been doing great damage for some months in a certain locality. We agreed with some reluctance, as we had intended going to another spot where we knew tigers were fairly numerous, but at the same time we were keen on trying our luck for a few days with a man-eater, which is not usually bagged in the same way as a civilised tiger. We got news of him immediately, as he followed our baggage carts for a few hundred yards within a mile and a half of our camp. The villagers emphatically told us that the man-eater would not touch a bait, but we tied out four young buffaloes, as there were said to be a couple of other tigers in that locality. The next morning we saw the shikari and others returning to camp minus one buffalo. We were filled with joy assuming that there had been a kill. But we knew from the faces of the shikari and the men as soon as they came near that something had gone wrong. Their story was that when they approached the third bait, which was tied about a sixty yards the other side of a deep nullish, they walked up to about fifteen yards of the buffalo, which was standing up, when they saw a tiger seated under a bush within ten feet of the bait. It was then about 8 a.m. The men (seven of them) formed a bunch, and they and the tiger stared at each other for a few seconds; the men then retired backwards till they reached the nullish, from which place they did sprints in record time!

label: paragraph_title
text: THE TIGER'S CUNNING

label: text
text: We went quickly to the spot, where we found the young buffalo still alive and without a scratch on him, and foot-prints of the tiger about four feet from the bait. We also saw the place where he had been sitting and the direction in which he had gone. The cunning brute would not touch the bait, but had sat there waiting for the men to come for it some time. Fortunately for the men the tiger was visible from the direction in which they came, otherwise they would have walked up to the buffalo without seeing him and there would certainly have been a tragedy.

label: text
text: Now ordinarily one would have expected a tiger, particularly a man-eater, to have attacked the men when they had gone so close to him. Two bounds would have reached them, but he did not move a muscle. On discussing the matter with the villagers they told us that the man-eater never attacked when he had been seen, and that he always got his victim unawares from behind. We did not get a chance at that brute, as he moved from that locality after a couple of days, evidently having got suspicious. This was believed to be the same man-eater which attacked Mr. George, the Divisional Forest Officer, in November last.

label: text
text: On a previous shoot my beaters were going through the jungle to the place from where the beat was to commence, when they suddenly came on to four tigers—male, female, and two nearly full-grown cubs, seated in the shade of a tree.

label: text
text:
The tiger kept roaring and charging towards the men, who stood their ground, while the tigress led the cubs away. Had all four tigers charged the men with the intention of doing damage; they would have made quite a good "bug." This beat was ruined for that day, but the next day those four tigers were beaten out. The tigress led the cubs and the tiger formed the rearg-guard. It was a hot day and the tigers were apparently not inclined to travel. The tiger kept only about 25 or 30 yards in front of the beaters, and frequently tapped round and growled and snarled at them, but did nothing more. He did not charge the beaters at all. The sad part of this story is that I tried to bring off a "right" and left us one does with snipe, and hit the tigress and one of the cubs, both of which got away!
ATTACKING CARTBULLOCKS.
About a couple of years ago a notorious old cattle-lifter in the south Central Provinces turned his attention to cart bullocks, which he found so easy to get. He is said

label: paragraph_title
text: ROYAL ENCLOSURE.

label: text
text: COVETED PRIVILEGE. AT ASCOT MEETING.

label: text
text:
Every year in the merry month of May appears in the newspapers. a short paragraph calculated to make those whose social achievements have not equalled their social ambitions anything but merry. Its wording is always precisely the same, and it is as follows:—
The list for Ascot Royal Enclosure tickets closes on—, and no applications can be considered after that date. They should be addressed to Viscount Churchill, Ascot Office, St. James's Palace, S.W. 1.
After that, says a writer in the "Sunday Express," the fully-qualified and the unqualifiable are alike in the outer darkness, for whom there is no hope. It is possible, of course, to make too much of these things, and most people to whom Ascot is a big event do so. But, on the principle that only those clubs are worth joining which are difficult to join, a badge for the Royal Enclosure at Ascot is worth considerably more than its weight, in gold to those who are uncertain of getting one.

label: paragraph_title
text: QUALIFIED CLUBs.

label: text
text: There is a large standing list to whom budgets come as night succeeds day to whom the Royal Enclosure in Asvot week is as natural as Eton for a school, and Christmas pudding on December 25.

label: text
text: The accepted method of application is to write, in the third person, to Lord Churchill from one of the list of qualified clubs. What those qualified clubs are, the members of them know full well. Others for th, most part, need not worry. As the space of the royal enclosure is limited and the number of those who cannot well be refused admission is large indeed, neither the place nor Lord Churchill's task grows in comfort each year.

label: paragraph_title
text: CROOK INTRUDER.

label: text
text: Perhaps the most extraordinary intruder to this strip of lawn was a notorious eagle, who, in 1914, impersonated a member of a foreign embassy, and walked about the enclosure in a false beard, fearing only lest it should rain. He took all "the ring" on, and was discovered on the third day. The affair came to the ears of the King some weeks later, and his Mlaesty insisted on a prosecution, which was abandoned because war broke out.

label: text
text:
But the vast majority of those who obtain badges are worthy to be the personal guests of the King and Queen, as in a sense, they are. Indeed, the Queen has been known to exercise her authority in the matter of women in the enclosure smoking or betting over the rails.
“If they want to help, their men must do it for them,” her Majesty is declared on good authority to have said.

label: text
text:
to have taken altogether nearly forty bullocks and buffaloes from carts moving along a certain section of a road, and carts ceased to ply on that road. He would drag the bullocks, from the cart a few yards into the jungle and there start his meal. On one occasion a driver hit the tiger with a stick several times on the head and body while he was attacking his bullock, but the tiger did not turn on him. The cartmen on some occasions followed the tiger with his kill into the jungle and tried to frighten him off, but he merely sat and growled and snarled at them. He did not on any occasion attempt to attack a man, either in a cart or in the jungle. I went after this brute once, but he slipped out of the beat. He was eventually shot, I believe, by a native shikari.
In the southern parts of the Central Provinces where tigers are fairly numerous, I have found that the villagers are not in the least afraid, when there are two or three of them, to go through the jungles even by night. Of course when there is a man-eater in the locality the men move about in larger batches and then only in broad daylight.

label: text
text: I could give some more instances, but it would make this letter too long. From my own experiences, however, and from genuine incidents which I have heard of, I have come to the conclusion that the tiger/like all animals, has a natural fear of man, and is ordinarily not dangerous, and that even a man-eater will probably not attack if he has been seen. Of course a wounded tiger is a different thing altogether. A tiger has a big "yellow streak" running through his nature and is not a "noble" animal like the lion. Any large wild animal may attack at times seemingly without provocation. I have known a large wild boar to charge a man at night, but a boar at the best of times is an aggressive beast. I have also known a wounded plug bull to charge, but he may have done so more from fright than anything else as ordinarily they are timid animals. The reason why all big game shooting is so fascinating is because of the glorious uncertainty as to what is going to happen.

label: paragraph_title
text: STEAM PLANES.

label: text
text: GREATER POWER, BUT LIGHTER ENGINES.

label: text
text: Dr. John S. Haldana, the president of the Institute of Mining Engineers, in a paper read at the annual meeting of the institute at Cardiff, said that some people seem to believe that the use of coal for steam engines was going to be more or less superseded. He believed that steam engines in the future, and the not very remote future, where steam was raised by coal or oil, would take the place of internal combustion engines in a great many cases.

label: text
text: In the case of the steam engine they had to jacket every part of it to retain the heat, but in the internal combustion engine they had to adopt other measures to get rid of the heat, otherwise the steel would not stand the temperatures to which it was subjected. This was a waste of heat energy.

label: text
text: The future development of the steam engine would be along the lines of increased steam pressure with smaller and lighter engines. The boilers also would be reduced in size as the pressure went up, so that the complete engine and boiler would be much smaller and lighter than an equivalent internal combustion engine, and would in all probability be more suitable and even superior for use in neocolumans and motor-cars.

label: text
text: The team engine would eventually beat the internal combustion engine.
